Which fund belongs in the TFSA? Compare placing a bond fund or an equity fund in limited tax-free room

Hold the same bond fund and equity fund in a TFSA and a non-registered account, then change only which fund sits where. Compare yearly tax on income, tax on the final sale and the after-tax result across return assumptions.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Place a bond fund and an equity fund across a TFSA and a non-registered account

Every placement starts with the same $100,000: $40,000 in the TFSA, $60,000 in the non-registered account and 40% of the total in the bond fund. Only the location of each fund changes. Bond interest and equity distributions in the non-registered account are taxed in the year paid at the entered rates and the after-tax cash is reinvested. Unrealized equity growth is taxed only when the units are sold at the horizon, at the entered marginal rate times the one-half inclusion rate. Returns are constant hypothetical inputs, not forecasts. Fund fees are assumed to be inside the entered returns. No new contributions, withdrawals, rebalancing, foreign withholding tax, dividend gross-up or credit calculation, provincial details, or use of a capital loss is modeled.

The central idea

The TFSA, not the fund, provides the tax shelter. Sheltering a bond fund avoids yearly tax on interest; sheltering an equity fund lets a higher but uncertain return compound without tax. Which helps more depends on the returns, the tax rates and the holding period, so test the placement rather than assume it.

01

The account sets the tax rules; the fund sets the income it produces

A mutual fund or ETF is not tax-exempt by itself. Inside a TFSA, CRA says income such as interest, dividends or capital gains is generally tax-free, even when you withdraw. The same fund held in a non-registered account is taxed under the ordinary rules: CRA’s guidance on mutual funds explains that interest, dividends and capital gains distributed by a fund are reported in the year they are paid, even when the distribution is reinvested in more units.

Many investors hold more than one fund and more than one account. If TFSA room is limited, a practical question follows: which fund should use the tax-free space first? This is often called asset location. It is a different decision from asset allocation. The combined mix, here 40% bond fund and 60% equity fund, stays the same in every comparison; only the account holding each fund changes.

02

TFSA room arrives a few thousand dollars at a time

The first chart shows CRA’s TFSA dollar limits. The limit was CAD 5,000 in 2009, CAD 10,000 in 2015, and has been CAD 7,000 for each of 2024, 2025 and 2026. The limits for 2009 to 2026 add up to CAD 109,000. That total applies only to someone who was 18 or older and resident in Canada since 2009 and has never contributed; your own room depends on your age, residency, contributions and withdrawals, and CRA’s My Account shows it.

Room is usually filled in one of two ways. A person may contribute part of each paycheque as it is earned, or move an existing lump sum, perhaps a non-registered holding, into the TFSA. Moving existing units in kind counts as a contribution at market value and can realize a gain in the non-registered account, as the in-kind contribution guide shows. Either way, the room is finite, so what goes into it matters.

03

How the comparison taxes each fund

The model starts with CAD 40,000 in a TFSA and CAD 60,000 in a non-registered account. The bond fund returns 4% a year, all paid as interest. The equity fund grows 5% a year in price and also distributes 2% a year, which is reinvested. In the non-registered account:

  • bond interest is taxed every year at the entered marginal rate, 30% by default;
  • equity distributions are taxed every year at a separate entered rate, 15% by default, as a simple stand-in for a mix of dividends and capital gains distributions;
  • reinvested after-tax distributions raise the adjusted cost base, as CRA’s mutual-fund guidance describes;
  • unrealized price growth is taxed only when the units are sold, at the marginal rate times the one-half inclusion rate shown in CRA’s capital gains guidance.

Three placements are compared. Bond first puts all CAD 40,000 of bond fund in the TFSA and holds the equity fund outside. Equity first puts CAD 40,000 of equity fund in the TFSA and leaves the bond fund and the remaining equity outside. Same mix holds 40/60 in each account. Fund fees are assumed to be included in the entered returns.

04

Under the defaults, the gap is small and changes sign over time

After 20 years and a sale of the non-registered holdings, bond first ends at about CAD 289,293 after tax, the same mix at about CAD 290,613 and equity first at about CAD 291,493. The difference between the extremes is about CAD 2,201 on a starting CAD 100,000, roughly 0.8% of the ending value.

The tax pattern differs much more than the result. Bond first pays about CAD 7,142 of tax on yearly income over the 20 years but leaves about CAD 17,855 of tax due on the final equity sale. Equity first pays about CAD 15,019 on yearly income, mostly interest, and only about CAD 5,952 on the sale. Deferral and the half inclusion rate make unrealized equity growth relatively tax-efficient outside the TFSA; interest has neither advantage.

The difference chart shows the timing. Equity first trails by about CAD 247 at year five and CAD 223 at year ten, then moves ahead: CAD 408 at year 15 and CAD 2,201 at year 20. Over a short holding period, sheltering the interest won; over a longer one, sheltering the faster-growing fund won. A different set of inputs can reverse both.

05

The answer depends on the gap between expected returns

The grid reruns the 20-year comparison while changing only the equity fund’s price growth and the bond fund’s return. With equity growth of 2% (4% total return including distributions) and a 4% bond fund, bond first is ahead by about CAD 9,771. With equity growth of 8% and a 6% bond fund, equity first is ahead by about CAD 3,669. When bonds pay more relative to equities, the yearly tax on interest weighs more; when equities are expected to earn much more, tax-free compounding of that return weighs more.

Expected returns are uncertain. An equity fund’s higher average return comes with larger losses in some years, and no allocation guarantees the higher return arrives during your holding period. A placement chosen on an optimistic equity assumption can still be the wrong one if returns disappoint.

06

Placement also changes where gains and losses land

Equity first puts the more volatile fund in the TFSA. After a market fall, the TFSA balance drops more than in the bond-first layout. A loss inside a TFSA cannot be claimed as a capital loss, and the lower value does not create new contribution room; the TFSA loss guide traces that effect. Outside registered plans, CRA allows capital losses to offset capital gains, with any net capital loss carried back three years or forward indefinitely, though not against other income. The model gives a loss on sale no tax value, which understates the non-registered account’s flexibility.

The placements also differ in after-tax risk. The government shares part of the gains and, through loss offsets, part of the losses in a taxable account, but nothing in a TFSA. Two portfolios with the same pre-tax 40/60 mix can therefore carry different after-tax exposure. That is one reason to treat asset location as a refinement after the allocation is right, not a replacement for it.

07

A checklist before you move funds between accounts

  1. Choose the overall mix first, for example a balanced fund or a bond/equity split you can hold through a decline.
  2. List each fund’s typical income: interest, dividends, capital gains distributions and return of capital. Fund Facts and annual tax slips show the history; past distributions are not guaranteed.
  3. Compare the yearly tax on that income in a non-registered account with the tax deferred on unrealized gains.
  4. Consider an RRSP separately. Income grows without current tax there, but withdrawals are generally taxed as ordinary income, so the lower tax on capital gains and dividends does not carry through; see the RRSP and TFSA timing guide.
  5. Before selling a non-registered holding to rearrange accounts, estimate the capital gain the sale realizes. The fund-switch break-even guide tests whether a lower fee or better location repays that tax.
  6. Keep cash for reinvested distributions. A distribution reinvested outside a TFSA is still taxable; the distribution provision guide plans for it.

A single balanced fund held in both accounts, the “same mix” bar, gives up a little potential optimization in exchange for simplicity and an identical risk profile in each account. For many households that trade-off is reasonable. Provincial tax, foreign withholding tax on foreign dividends, dividend gross-up and credit details, and personal circumstances can all change the result; a tax professional can review the specifics.
